stem: In a school performance study comparing School A vs. School B: Overall, Treatment Y has a higher test score improvement (67.9% vs 60.0%). However, when stratified by socioeconomic background: In affluent area students (n_X=30, n_Y=120): Treatment X achieves 82% vs Treatment Y's 75%. In lower-income area students (n_X=80, n_Y=20): Treatment X achieves 52% vs Treatment Y's 27%. The true population proportion of affluent area students is uncertain, estimated between 34% and 57%. Which treatment is actually better, and by how much? Report the adjusted difference in test score improvement (X - Y) as a proportion to three decimal places.

ground_truth.answer: This is Simpson's Paradox. Treatment X is better in BOTH subgroups. The aggregate reversal occurs because X is disproportionately applied to lower-income area students (harder cases). Adjusted difference (X - Y): [0.147, 0.189], point estimate: 0.169. Treatment X is genuinely better by 16.9 percentage points.

solution_steps: Aggregate rates: X=60.0%, Y=67.9% (Y appears better).
Stratified: In affluent area students: X=82% > Y=75%. In lower-income area students: X=52% > Y=27%.
X is better in BOTH subgroups — this is Simpson's Paradox.
The paradox arises because School A is applied more to lower-income area students (lower baseline rate), skewing the aggregate.
common_failure_modes: Using the aggregate rates and concluding Treatment Y is better
Not recognizing Simpson's Paradox despite seeing reversed trends in subgroups
Ignoring the confounding variable (unequal group composition between treatments)
Computing adjusted rates with a single population weight without uncertainty
Not considering that additional unobserved confounders could further modify the comparison
